name: Life at a Hardware Startup

claims.claim_text: Venture-funded chip and EDA startups generally operate under an implicit exit strategy rather than a plan to become an independent long-term vendor: the investors who supplied the money need a return and press for the company to be sold as soon as possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're under the pump. The venture capitalists are the ones who gave you the money and they want to make their return. They want to sell it back as soon as possible.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Holding out for smaller investments preserves control, because the majority shareholder decides company policy; once a founder's stake is diluted to a few percent through public or later-round funding, the shareholders rather than the founder set direction.
claims.quote_verbatim: the majority shareholder, if Mark Zuckerberg is the majority shareholder in Facebook, that means he gets to call the shots. And as soon as, as soon as they go public to get money and he's now down to like two or 5% shares of the shares rather than, yeah, sorry, sorry, buddy.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: Cree's founders raised their initial capital entirely from friends and family, in individual cheques of around $5,000 written informally rather than through any institutional investor.
claims.quote_verbatim: It was basically talking to friends and family, going to a bar and sit there and someone writes you a check for $5,000. And it was some other folks. It was all family and friends, basically.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with John Edmond - Luciferous LED Lucubrator

claims.claim_text: Stock granted to early startup employees has no realisable value unless the company either floats or is acquired; absent a liquidity event there is no market in which to sell it.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you go work at a startup right you know you risk everything go work at the start and they give you a shitload of stock and uh well that stock's worthless unless the company either floats or maybe gets bought out in some way shape
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Local economic-development bodies and private foundations in some regions fund startups with comparatively few strings attached, their objective being to keep businesses in the region rather than to take equity; founders are advised to look for this localised money before assuming venture capital is the only source.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, if you're thinking about a startup, look for that kind of localized funding, because it's possible. And even if not that, maybe even national stuff, because there's, you know, STEM programs and stuff like that. There's a lot of... There is funding out there. It's not easy to get, but it's out there.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Studies of startup founders find successful founders skew older than the popular image: roughly twice as many successful founders are over 50 as under 25, and twice as many over 60 as under 20.
claims.quote_verbatim: We found twice as many successful founders over 50 as under 25, and twice as many over 60 as under 20, which means that it skews higher.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: One hardware campaign structured its reward tiers to avoid the kit-assembly audience entirely, offering bare PCBs at a token $20 level, assembled PCBs for backers who wanted to save money and spare the team labour, and a fully hand-assembled final unit with cut acrylic, aluminium washers and a getting-started kit.
claims.quote_verbatim: We offered bare PCBs just for sort of a token thanks for your $20. Or we offered assembled PCBs for people who wanted to save some money and save us some hassle. And then we offered the final unit with the laboriously hand-assembled, cut acrylic, aluminum washers. You get the idea. Rubber feet. With a whole getting started kit with a whole $2 of components and nice jumper wires.
claims.speaker: Ian Danaher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: Delaying a venture round while building the company on the founders' own money improves the valuation, so the same sum of investment buys the investor a much smaller share — on the order of ten percent instead of fifty.
claims.quote_verbatim: the better pricing you will get. So if they give you a certain sum of money, right, they will get a smaller share. Oh, they'll get a smaller percentage, right. Yes, exactly. They'll get 10% instead of 50%.
claims.speaker: Oyvind Janbu
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunded hardware efforts fall into three bands: the barely funded one-off, the outlier that raises millions and becomes a full-time company, and a middle band described as the pit of despair, where the money is too little to hire a team but the obligation is large enough to consume the founder's life.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then he called the middle one the pit of despair. And it's interesting. It's the pit of despair where you haven't got enough money to hire a team of people to take care of it for you, and then you don't have to worry about it. And where you have to... So you have to do everything, and you're working 24-7, and your marriage falls down
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: Designers avoid specifying parts from chip startups without a compelling reason, because the odds of the vendor failing are high and the part may not exist in five years — a structural obstacle for any startup selling silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm not going to go out and, uh, use a chip from a startup and unless I absolutely have to like the, you know, there's some massively compelling reason to do it. Um, just because yeah, the odds of them failing are quite large and that part not being there in five years time is, you know, is very, you know, the odds of that is very large.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Tektronix, ChipReport.tv, & the Signal Path - Temperative Tegmen Temperature

claims.claim_text: Bank debt for a design-and-build business is secured personally: the founder signs over their house and gives personal guarantees, so the entrepreneur, not the bank, carries the downside risk.
claims.quote_verbatim: You still have a bank, and, you know, don't get me started on banks, but let's just say that, you know, my firstborn was signed over. Oh, right. Along to my house and everything else.
claims.speaker: Larry Sears
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Larry Sears - Hexagram Hardware Holism

claims.claim_text: Entering medium-volume consumer hardware typically requires between two and ten million dollars of funding, which in practice comes from venture investors who expect defensible intellectual property — a direct tension for companies that want to be open source.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need anywhere from, you know, two to probably more like 10 million of funding. Which usually will come through a VC or group of VCs. And I think they would probably be concerned how do they protect their IP and make money on this. Of course. If it's all open. So, the trick is just that how do you get funding for something that's substantial?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Accelerators change the investment decision from a one- or two-week judgement on a pitch into a three- to six-month observation period, during which investors watch how a founding team functions under stress, handles obstacles and pivots before committing funds.
claims.quote_verbatim: rather than looking at a pitch and having to decide in a week or two whether you want to commit significant funds to this, you have the course of three months or six months to really get to know the entrepreneurs, see how they function as a team, see how they handle stress. How do they overcome obstacles? How do they pivot?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Hardware accelerators are structured to bring a team to the point of being fundable by venture investors, which in turn shapes what they select for: businesses capable of high volume or of reaching roughly $100 million in scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: And all of these accelerators are really looking at truly accelerating a team to a point where they'll be fundable. And thinking about what the VCs want to fund. They want to, in most cases, fund high volume or to get to that $100 million business.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Venture investors in a hardware company are not aiming at a twenty- or fifty-million-dollar outcome but at a five-hundred-million or billion-dollar one, and that target drives decisions such as closing a previously open design.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't want this to be a $20 million company. They don't want it to be a $50 million company. They want it to be a $500 million or a billion dollar company
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: Pricing a hardware product by taking the bill-of-materials cost and adding a fixed markup of around twenty percent does not produce a viable business; margins have to be calculated to cover the whole cost structure, not just parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of people approach this with the point of view of you look at your bomb cost and then I'll add 20% or something for your margin and that just doesn't work that way.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Investors in consumer-electronics companies frequently will not engage below roughly ten million dollars of scale, leaving smaller open-source hardware companies in a gap between being too small for investment and too small to act like a large company.
claims.quote_verbatim: They won't even talk to you if you're less than 10 million, they said. And 10 million, that is non-trivial. That is a big milestone. Yeah, exactly. That's a big one of cash.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: Venture firms sometimes recruit a founder through an entrepreneur-in-residence arrangement: the firm pays the individual, provides an office and access to its contacts inside and outside venture capital, in the expectation that they will start a company the firm finds interesting — though the firm is under no obligation to fund it.
claims.quote_verbatim: what they do in some cases is they bring on somebody like myself as what's called an entrepreneur in residence. And what they do is they'll pay you and you'll get an office. You'll get all their contacts inside of venture capital and out with the concept being that you're going to start a company that's interesting to them. They may or may not fund it at the end of the day.
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: When the venture firm that sponsored an entrepreneur-in-residence declines to fund the resulting company, the refusal itself becomes a black mark with other investors, who ask why the sponsoring firm passed; the founders then face the ordinary pitch grind regardless.
claims.quote_verbatim: And it turned out the VC firm I was working with didn't end up funding us. Oh, wow. And that ends up actually being – yeah. So it ends up actually being a negative because of various things. Because it's like, why didn't they fund you? And there are many different reasons that VC companies don't fund people. And it turned out in this particular instance that had nothing to do with us. But it ends up being kind of a black mark. So the other war stories that you just heard about, you know, hundreds of VC firms and everything else, we went through all that.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Foundries are selective about direct startup business because they expect to lose money on any startup, treating the engagement as an investment of their time; a fabless startup's access therefore depends heavily on personal relationships held by its investors and board.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I work with a TSMC, for example, you know, TSMC is very picky about who they do business with. And if they want to do business with you directly, they want to be convinced that it's worth their time because what they'll tell you is on any startup, they're going to lose money. So it's an investment for them and their time.
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Founding a business to eliminate a task one hates is self-defeating, because the founder ends up doing that task continuously as the core of the business.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you start a business, to deal with something that you hate doing, it turns out that you end up doing that all of the time
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: An accelerator batch culminates in a demo day at which each company gives a short pitch to investors; the actual fundraising happens in the weeks following that event rather than on the day itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: then in the end of that, you do, uh, what's called demo day, which is, uh, where, where you, um, present to investors. Um, and, uh, that, that is basically, you know, you, you, you do a very short pitch and you, you explain to people, uh, what it is that you're doing and, you know, um, hopefully you've got some business behind what, what you're doing. Um, and, uh, from that, you then, uh, you then attempt to raise investment in the kind of weeks, uh, the weeks after demo day.
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: Running a kit business at maximum profit by packing and shipping every unit yourself converts the venture into a permanent twelve-hour-a-day job: revenue can be reasonable but margin per unit is thin and the labour never ends.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you go into the kit, kit business and you're making the maximum profit packing and shipping each one. Well, yeah, congratulations. You've just scored yourself a 12 hour a day job for the rest of your life. You know? Yeah. You might be making a, you know, quite a lot of money, but not like a lot of margin, but you're working your ass off.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, IndieGoGo & Ignite - Jasperated Jimswinger Jobbery

claims.claim_text: MakerBot's move from a 5,000 to a 50,000 square foot facility was funded by venture investment, not retained profit; incremental bootstrapping does not deliver an order-of-magnitude jump in production scale, which is the core reason capital-hungry hardware companies take outside money.
claims.quote_verbatim: Just take a look at MakerBot, right? They just opened a 50,000 square foot facility, right? They went from 5,000 square feet to 50,000 square feet, right? How did they do, how did they afford to do that? Well, it was their venture capital investment, right? They really couldn't have, you know, gone on that sort of scale just by, you know, the small profit margin they're making. Oh, yeah. I'm not sure how big they are, but, you know, just that continual bootstrapping thing doesn't get you, you know, that order of magnitude gain in the production scale that you're after.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: The practical difference between angel and venture investors is cheque size and usefulness: angels write smaller cheques but tend to be more helpful, while venture funds write larger ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, nothing. It's the size of the checks they write. Angels tend to be more useful. VCs tend to write bigger checks.
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Angel investors typically expect a return across a portfolio and invest partly for non-financial reasons, whereas venture funds invest solely to make money; the distinction is between someone whose job is investing and someone whose hobby is.
claims.quote_verbatim: VCs are only doing it to make money. Right. And that's, so, like, that's the really big difference between the two is you're working with somebody whose job is investing versus somebody whose hobby is investing.
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: A software-for-hardware company that ran three years at an average of seven people with effectively zero sales accumulated roughly a million dollars of payroll before any revenue, a sum no ordinary founding team can fund personally — the defining case for a non-bootstrappable business.
claims.quote_verbatim: We've been, like, our sales are effectively zero. It's been three years. And we've been an average of seven people, right? So, like, run that payroll. Yeah. And, you know, you're at a million dollars paid up front for a thing that doesn't make any money.
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Hardware startup founders are rarely straight out of school; most have prior industry experience, in contrast to the young-founder pattern common in software.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of them have some sort of industry experience. You know, it's not like they come, you know, straight out of graduate school and bam, into it.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Prior Art, Wafer Fabs and Guns - Whimsical Wafer Waffling

claims.claim_text: Wayne and Layne began in autumn 2009 with each founder contributing about $300 to build a hundred units of a single kit, an outlay small enough that failure would merely leave a lifetime supply of parts; growing slowly from there, the company was later selling tens of thousands of its Blinkies units to retailers.
claims.quote_verbatim: we started in 2009, the fall of 2009. And we put in like 300 bucks each to make like 100 of one kit. And we said, well, if this fails, we'll just have a lifetime supply of, of this certain pick and this PCB and it'll be like no big deal. Yeah. And then, I mean, last year with our Blinkies, we sold tens of thousands of our Blinkies to retailers.
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: A million dollars of funding buys roughly five people for one year in a company that is not yet manufacturing, a useful rule for judging how much runway a crowdfunding or seed sum actually represents.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's five people if you're not building stuff or if you're not manufacturing. That's five people for a year.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: One augmented-reality startup planned from the outset to use a strong Kickstarter result as leverage for a later venture round, having first pitched investors before the campaign and been offered money only in exchange for a large share of the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: that was actually part of our plan from day one, a strong showing on Kickstarter. And before Kickstarter, we went to a bunch of venture capitalists and showed them the product. And, of course, they came back like, yeah, we'll give you some money, but, you know, we want a big chunk of your company.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Venture investors routinely open by asking how many patents a company holds, which pushes founders to file patents they would not otherwise pursue simply to make the company look attractive.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's part of the VC thing, though. The first thing they ask you is how many patents you have.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: A patent costs on the order of $10,000 to obtain but around $100,000 to defend the first time, so for a startup the emphasis on intellectual property as a way of keeping competitors out is usually misplaced.
claims.quote_verbatim: what they say is $10,000 to get a patent. But $100,000 to defend it for the first time and then it's worth something.
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: The value of a product is the idea multiplied by the execution, so a strong idea executed poorly is worth little; in products shipping to customers, most of the execution effort belongs in the last ten percent of the project, which is where failure occurs.
claims.quote_verbatim: the value of something is really the idea times the execution. And if you have a great idea, but poor execution, that's not worth very much. And so learning to execute is critical. So, um. Right. And the, and the thing is, especially when you're executing on products that are going out to people is that 90% of your execution better be in the last 10% of that project because that's when it fails.
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: One founder moved to part-time and then quit his job before the product generated income, intending to fall back on consulting if it failed — a staged exit that limits risk without waiting for revenue.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I kind of switched to part-time and then quit with the hope that this would take, that something would happen, and I was kind of planning on doing consulting on the side or something. Not that I really had a plan for how to do that either, but it actually worked. So you actually quit before it was making you money?
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: A connected-device startup that raised roughly a quarter of a million dollars from family and friends, then failed to close a $2 million seed round, ran out of cash after about a year of development and shut down, publishing the underlying figures.
claims.quote_verbatim: they raised a quarter of a million bucks from family and friends. And they... Hang on. They tried to get a $2 million seed around.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: Adapteva would have gone bankrupt after trouble with its Kickstarter campaign had a large telecoms equipment maker and a venture investor not stepped in, a rescue that came at the cost of some control over the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: when we ran into trouble with the Kickstarter campaign, it was, uh, it was, uh, a Swedish company, a big base station company named Ericsson and, um, and a VC that saved us. So we, we would have, we would have gone, we would have gone bankrupt if it wasn't for them.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: When reaching a shipping product requires not just the hardware but a surrounding ecosystem — silicon, boards and software together — the multi-million-dollar cost puts the effort beyond what bootstrapping can fund.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you need millions of dollars to reach a product and an ecosystem, it's hard to do that. Just bootstrapping.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: A development board sold without the daughter cards and application solutions that make it useful scores zero commercially: the sale depends on the complete set being in place, and the third-party accessory ecosystem that grew around Arduino or Raspberry Pi only appears once a large customer base already exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: a board by itself without the daughter cards is still a zero score, right? So it's a, it's an end operation. You need all the things in place to make a successful sale.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: The bootstrapping loop for a small hardware product is concrete: buy parts for a hundred kits from saved money, sell those hundred, use the few thousand dollars of proceeds to buy more parts, and repeat; it works but is slow.
claims.quote_verbatim: Buy a hundred kits worth of parts. Sell your hundred kits. Make your, make, you know, I don't know, a few grand on it. Use that few grand to buy more parts and then more and then more. And you bootstrap it that way. And it takes time.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Founders face a direct trade between roles: someone who wants to keep doing engineering cannot also be the person raising money, and someone who wants to run the company must take on fundraising as the job.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you want to keep being an engineer, you don't get to go hunting for money. If you want to be in charge, you've got to go hunt for the money
claims.speaker: Ahmed

claims.claim_text: Raising money is not a side activity: founders who have secured funding typically describe roughly twelve months of full-time effort spent on it, so a founder pursuing investment generally has to give up other commitments for that period.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can't just do it on the side and think that, you know, somebody is just going to hand you money. It's like, you know, you, everyone we've spoken to, it's like, oh yeah, we've, you know, worked our ass off for, you know, 12 months trying to get somebody to fund us
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Investors do not fund ideas alone; a founder needs demonstrated progress beyond the concept before money is available.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you, you need more than just an idea. No one's going to give you money for an idea.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: One structural advantage of hardware over software as a business is that customers expect to pay for a physical product, so revenue does not depend on converting a free user base.
claims.quote_verbatim: people expect to pay for hardware, unlike software, for example, you know, really, really helps as a thing to build a business around when people expect to pay you for it.
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Y Combinator's standard offer at the time was approximately $20,000 for about seven percent of the company, with founders expected to be resident for the three-month batch.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're offered a spot, it's essentially $20,000 for what boils down to basically 7% of your company and your team. Founders are expected to be here for the three-month badge.
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: At the earliest prototype stage — before manufacturing and per-unit cost matter — a hardware startup should not be materially slower than a software one; obtaining populated PCBs or a 3D-printed enclosure should add at most about a week to any iteration.
claims.quote_verbatim: There should be few to no excuses for why a hardware startup at the very earliest stages, like ignoring manufacturing everything, because that often comes later. The very early stages on like ignoring your incremental cost per unit, there's very few things that a startup doing hardware cannot do nearly as quickly as a startup doing software. Like it should never take you more than an extra week, whether it's getting populated PCBs or a 3D printed enclosure or whatever.
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Making one, ten, a hundred and a thousand units are materially different problems, and separate again from establishing that anyone will buy them; the step most often skipped is selling ten units before scaling.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a big difference though, between making one of something, making 10 of something, make a hundred something, make it a thousand of something and understanding if people actually want to buy any of them in the first place. And so the first step is always sell 10 of them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A small startup often leaves a specialist engineer as the only person in their discipline, with no senior colleague to learn from; engineers seeking to deepen a specialism such as analogue generally need a team large enough to contain two or three practitioners of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's kind of the downside to a startup-type mentality of who do you learn from
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Founders normally hold common stock while venture investors hold preferred shares, which rank ahead in a liquidation; a founder can therefore retain a nominal fifty percent of a company and still receive nothing when it is wound up, because the preferred holders are paid first.
claims.quote_verbatim: she still doesn't own 50% of the revenue because she's a common stock shareholder and all the venture capitalists who invested money in it, they have a higher priority in the stock. They have a, what's the word? Preferred shares. They have preferred shares. They have preferred shares. Yeah. So they get the money first.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Large companies have committed roadmaps and resources and structurally cannot pursue risky unproven directions, which is why startups exist: they take the technical risk cheaply, and the few that succeed are acquired while most simply fail and disappear.
claims.quote_verbatim: a big company, you know, they've got engineers and they've got priorities, they've got roadmaps, and their resources are committed and they really can't afford to – it's not their business to take these risky steps out into unknown territory. Right. So as these startups are out there doing that, this kind of cloud of gnats, if you will, buzzing around, you know, taking advantage of all these opportunities, occasionally a few of them grow up and those are ripe for being consumed.
claims.speaker: Clint Cole
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Clint Cole of Digilent

claims.claim_text: An engineer who left a stable instrument company for a hardware startup found it out of money within four months, after which he continued working while accruing shares in place of salary — a common terminal state for an underfunded startup.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I went and joined a startup that, uh, was doing some hardware stuff and, and developing it. And, uh, they ran out of money like four months later. Uh, so they were, they were, they were toast like four months later. And, but I, and I stayed on afterwards, you know, accruing shares, um, instead of money.
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: A competing high-speed camera shipped despite usability compromises — no onboard display, Ethernet tethering to a computer and an external power supply — and sold around 700 units at $5,500 each, illustrating that a shipped imperfect product outperforms an unshipped better one.
claims.quote_verbatim: they made a few mistakes like not having an onboard LCD. You had to connect it by Ethernet to a computer and you needed to tether it to a power supply and it was a lot of effort to use. But apparently they've sold 700 of those at $5,500 each.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An engineer's unwillingness to sell a product he judges unfinished is the characteristic barrier between engineering and entrepreneurship; a business-minded founder ships through that barrier and raises money against it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I asked myself, would I be confident in selling this? No, I wouldn't. You're an engineer and not an entrepreneur.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A seed cheque of around $500,000 is large in absolute terms but small against the cost of building a hardware business, and companies that raised similar sums through crowdfunding have gone bust for want of enough capital.
claims.quote_verbatim: we'll write 500K checks, which is a lot. But at the same time, it's not very much in the grand scheme of getting a business built. More importantly… You don't necessarily do a lot with 500K. A lot of people think that's a lot. But you get 500K for a crowdfunding campaign and a lot of companies have gone bust because they didn't get enough.
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: A crowdfunding campaign that raises three or four hundred thousand dollars is the beginning of a hardware company's risk exposure, not the end of it, although founders commonly read it as the moment they are clear.
claims.quote_verbatim: they might have, you know, raised 300, 400,000. And they think they're out of the woodwork. It's like they're just starting the risk level.
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Building a hardware startup compounds an unusual number of disciplines at once — product and platform, software, electrical and mechanical engineering, new product introduction, contract manufacturing, distribution, supply chain and logistics, and regulatory compliance such as UL, NSF and FCC certification — which is why investors treat it as the hardest category of venture.
claims.quote_verbatim: building a hardware startup is what we would call the triple black diamond of entrepreneurship, right? You're not only building a product, you're building a platform. You're writing software. You're designing hardware. You're going through electrical engineering, mechanical engineering. You have, you know, new product introduction. You have to deal with contract manufacturers. You then probably need to handle distribution, supply chain, logistics, compliance. I mean, you might need UL certification. You might need NSF certification. You might need to go through FCC certification.
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Many venture investors become uneasy about open-source hardware and ask about patent protection; some investors take the opposite view and treat a founder who leads with their patent portfolio as a warning sign, on the grounds that a patent position is not a business.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of VCs get scared when you're open source and they'll ask, you know, they'll be like, Oh, what's your patent protection? What does your patent portfolio look like? And I push entrepreneurs. If an entrepreneur comes to me and early, early on in the conversation starts telling me about their patents, I basically look at them and I say, I'm not here to fund a lawsuit.

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding pricing is set by the minimum order quantity a founder can afford: a $50 bill of materials at an MOQ of 500 units forces a $100 retail price, whereas an investor funding an MOQ ten times larger can drop the BOM cost enough to sell the same product at $75 and reach a wider audience.
claims.quote_verbatim: what happens if you go out and launch a campaign and you're like, all right, I'm going to sell this product for $100 because I think that the bill of materials is $50 because at a minimum order quantity of 500 units, I can get it for $50. Well, what if you had an investor behind the scenes who said, look, you should get MOQs that are 10 times that size. Like you should be going out and going bigger. Plan bigger. Yeah, yeah. And you then get to sell the product on Kickstarter for $75 at which point you might have a much broader audience to hit.
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: The overwhelming majority of products sold in mainstream retail were never venture-backed, so founders should decide deliberately whether they are building a venture-backable business or simply a good one; the latter is well served by a modest crowdfunding campaign followed by successive products.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you walk down the aisleways of Best Buy and Target and Walmart, 99.9% of those products are never venture-backed. They're just great products that were built. So we oftentimes urge people. We say, are you sure you want to build a venture-backable business or do you just want to build a great business?
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Venture capital is accelerant rather than ignition: it multiplies a business that is already burning, and pouring it on a venture too small to absorb it does not create growth.
claims.quote_verbatim: Venture capital is fuel that goes on a fire. And if you have a small little fire and you just want to add twigs to it and logs to it and bigger and bigger wood, you can build a fire over time. But if your fire isn't capable of accommodating some jet fuel, then don't pour jet fuel.
claims.speaker: Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: Engineers who work across mechanical, electrical and software domains tend to fit startups poorly at large companies, which pigeonhole staff into single specialisms, and correspondingly well at startups, where breadth is the requirement.
claims.quote_verbatim: You know, you had to do the mechanical stuff, the electrical stuff, the programming stuff, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. And that was very well suited to startups. You know, I worked for a couple of big companies, and, you know, they try to pigeonhole you to doing one thing, and that did not work well.
claims.speaker: Gerry Roston

claims.claim_text: Scaling a hardware company to production requires capital on two distinct fronts: cash to buy the bill of materials itself, and the continuing cost of engineering salaries, so a raise sized only against parts underestimates the requirement.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we need money just for the bill of materials is one thing. Yeah, right. But in addition to that, a big cost obviously is the engineering talent and salaries in general.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Component distributors have entered the crowdfunding-support market directly, with Arrow offering grants of around $75,000 to selected hardware projects alongside its parts supply.
claims.quote_verbatim: Arrow gives 75 grand to certain projects
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Selling a company does not necessarily leave the founder with money: in one case the structure of the sale produced a seven-figure tax bill and a net negative position for the founder despite a headline sale worth millions.
claims.quote_verbatim: the end result is that my net position is negative. So we ended up with a very big tax bill. So like seven figure tax bill to pay, that sort of thing, which is quite scary. So even though I've just sold a company, and technically you can say, oh, I've sold a company for millions of dollars. It's not like I'm sleeping on a pile of cash.
claims.speaker: Jon Oxer

claims.claim_text: A founder returning to the job market after decades of broad self-directed work can fail to qualify even for entry-level engineering postings, because those listings screen on narrow specific requirements such as five years of a single language rather than on breadth of shipped work.
claims.quote_verbatim: my particular circumstance is that I didn't actually finish university. And my experience since that time has been very broad. I've worked in hardware and in software and associated things as well. So as I was looking down this list, I found that even for entry level positions, I couldn't tick any of the boxes.
claims.speaker: Jon Oxer

claims.claim_text: Startup death is usually abrupt rather than gradual: the company operates normally until the remaining runway is measured in days and no further investment arrives, at which point it stops.
claims.quote_verbatim: they simply ran out of money and that's what happens. Like once the, like the money literally runs out overnight or, you know, like we've, we've got a week's worth of money left and there's no more investment.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Failing companies rarely disclose their position, because admitting to being near bankruptcy destroys any chance of a decent sale price — which is why outside observers see an apparently healthy company vanish overnight.
claims.quote_verbatim: nobody wants to admit to anyone that they're on the brink of bankruptcy. Cause you're always hoping. Right. Right. You can't be like, we're in trouble. We're in trouble. Cause then if you do sell, then you sell for a very poor price.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A light investor relationship can be worth more for the discipline it imposes than the capital: a quarterly request for financials obliges the founder to maintain an accountant, a bookkeeper and real profit and cash-flow statements.
claims.quote_verbatim: every quarter they email me and ask for the financials, um, which means I have to have financials. Like I have an accountant, I have a bookkeeper. Like we, we have profit, you know, cash flow statements, all, all that stuff.

claims.claim_text: Entrepreneurship in hardware is difficult to sustain in isolation; working out of a shared facility where others are doing the same is a practical way to pick up process knowledge that is not written down.
claims.quote_verbatim: entrepreneurship is tough. You don't do it in a vacuum. It's, it's difficult to do it in your own garage. You've got to go, go, go to a place like M hub in Chicago where there's people doing this and you can pick up some nuggets of wisdom.
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: Raising more money than a plan requires is itself a hazard: one company was making rapid progress on a $1.5 million seed round with ten people, then raised $15 million, grew to about twenty people, and found the investor expectation had shifted to burning cash quickly to accelerate.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it's also important to have, like, a really solid plan of how much money to raise. Like, I think we almost raised too much money because, you know, we raised $1.5 million in a seed round. Yeah. And we had, like, 10 people working for us, and we were making tons of progress. And then we raised $15 million. We only grew the team in the first six months to, like, 20-ish people. And we were still moving really fast. But the expectation was, after six months or so, it's like, you need to really be accelerating this company. And that's where you need to start burning this money fast.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: The venture funding cycle runs at roughly annual intervals: a round is sized to be exhausted in about a year, so a company still holding a large cash balance past that point is read by its investors as behind schedule rather than as prudent.
claims.quote_verbatim: We had something like $8 million in the bank when this transition happened and we'd been going for quite some time on that money. And the plan was, you know, to be out of money in a year ish. Right. So like your cycle in a startup is raising money every single year ish.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding stretch goals are a recognised failure mechanism: in one headphone project, adding mobile support expanded the software scope from two operating systems to five, added a 32-core on-board processor and required business development with handset makers, ultimately doubling the size of the development.
claims.quote_verbatim: The addition of stretch goals to add mobile support increased the software scope from two operating systems to five, added an incredibly powerful 32-core processor onboard for headphones for processing, and requires us to enter into substantial business development with mobile manufacturers to support multi-channel connectivity. It ultimately doubled the size of our development.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Around 2011 and 2012 most venture investors regarded hardware as a poor investment relative to software and social media, and were dismissive of funds intending to back physical products.
claims.quote_verbatim: Most VCs thought hardware was stupid. Uh, and this is whatever, 2011, 2012. That's direct. Yeah, I think it's true. And I think most people think, uh, you know, SAS and social media were sort of like the big thing at the time. Um, it probably still are in many ways. And they were kind of, um, they gave less sort of, uh, credence to the value of building things physical. And so they were pretty dismissive as VCs often are.
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Because of how management fees and fund structures work, a first-time fund is often better raised from individuals — including partners at other funds writing personal cheques — than from institutional funds themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: because of management fees and some other sort of more nuanced topics about how, how venture funds operate. You actually, uh, in many cases don't want to raise money from, uh, funds. You, you do want to raise money from individuals. And sometimes those individuals are partners at funds.
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: A venture fund is a trust relationship in which limited partners supply nearly all the capital and hold very little control, general partners supply little capital and hold most of the control, and in exchange the limited partners take most of the financial upside.
claims.quote_verbatim: the limited partner puts in all the money and has very little control. Uh, and the general partner puts in very little money and has, uh, you know, very much control. Uh, and so it's really a trust relationship between the LPs and the GPs. Uh, and the trade-off for that is the LPs get most of the financial upside.
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: A business selling a physical widget at twenty to thirty points of gross margin is intrinsically hard to sustain, which is the underlying reason hardware was historically underfunded by venture investors; the category became fundable when hardware was reframed as a delivery mechanism for software.
claims.quote_verbatim: selling a widget for, you know, 20, 30 points of, of, of gross margin dollars, uh, is, is really challenging as a business in today's day and age. There are a few companies that can do it.
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: A hardware-focused seed investor's cheques ranged from roughly $100,000 to $150,000 at the low end up to $500,000 or $750,000, sized according to the company's progress and the investors' confidence in the founders.
claims.quote_verbatim: that investment ranges probably the, you know, on the low end, uh, we'll write a, you know, a hundred or $150,000 check. Uh, and, and we will write larger checks, um, you know, 500,000 and $750,000, uh, depending on again, the progress of the company
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Venture returns require outlier outcomes — typically around $100 million of annual revenue within five to seven years — so an investor declining a company usually means it does not fit that revenue-and-timeline model, not that the product is poor.
claims.quote_verbatim: which are big businesses, uh, doing, you know, typically in some number of years, five to seven years doing, you know, a hundred million dollars of revenue or more
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: The staffing sequence for a hardware startup runs generalists first — broad engineers who can get something working end-to-end — and specialist experts only once funding is secured or clearly forthcoming, because experts are expensive and each requires supporting staff around them.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's good to have people are generally good at first. And then like yourself, Chris, and then who can kind of do a lot of different things. And then you get it to a point where you have funding or it's clear you're going to get it. Or, um, or so some night point wherein it's worth, then you get the experts. You, you have to pay for them. They're not cheap, but you get the experts in and they make it better.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gregory Charvat and Three New Companies

claims.claim_text: A technical founding team should recruit a capable business person early to incorporate the company, handle the legal work, identify the target market and take on fundraising, on the principle that engineers should be honest about what they are not good at.
claims.quote_verbatim: And you always need a very good business person to help you set the company up, to help you find the market. The legal piece. Do the legal piece. There's a lot there. Yep. So he found that person. Yep. And that's the person that will raise the money as well
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: Gregory Charvat and Three New Companies

claims.claim_text: A lifestyle business — comfortable, interesting and self-sustaining — runs directly against the prevailing entrepreneurial doctrine, which pushes founders toward a growth business that can be built and then walked away from as passive income.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like building a lifestyle business. It's like comfortable. Yeah. Yeah. There's a lot of interesting problems, but not like a growth business. But it's very anti-entrepreneurial.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: For a startup raising $20-80 million with a steep burn rate, spending on the order of a hundred thousand dollars to build a patent portfolio is a rational cost: patents function as value signalling to investors and acquirers, and if the company fails the money was lost anyway.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're raising, you know, 20 to $80 million and you're going to, you know, you've got a, a really steep burn and you're really trying to make something really big, you know, to, to, to put a hundred thousand dollars or whatever into developing a patent portfolio is probably pretty wise and your investors are going to love it.

claims.claim_text: Technical seed investors select for founders who bring half-disassembled prototypes and want to discuss implementation detail, rather than for business-degree founders with polished pitch decks.
claims.quote_verbatim: the people that really resonate with us are the ones who walk into our office with like, you know, half disassembled prototypes that want to geek out about, you know, the algorithms that they're running on the Cortex M7. Like, it's, you know, people that are, love to geek out on the technical details and that are deeply, deeply technical people. And not people that come in with like business degrees and super polished pitch decks.
claims.speaker: Chrissy Meyer

claims.claim_text: A hardware company can reach a hundred million dollars of annual revenue and still fail, because taking too much investment capital sets a required outcome the revenue cannot satisfy; when investors stop believing that outcome is reachable, funding ends and the company closes almost immediately.
claims.quote_verbatim: How do they lose money? It's just the same way. Patreon are going to go bankrupt if they can't, you know, get other sources. You know, how do you lose money? It's because you took too much. Yeah. You took too much. They took too much. Patreon took too much. Tons of companies have taken too much investment capital.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A media business with 125,000 magazine subscribers still failed while smaller competitors ran profitably, in part because it had taken around ten million dollars of venture capital early on and venture investors require roughly a tenfold return.
claims.quote_verbatim: They took 10 million bucks that we know about, right? Way, way back at the start. They took, and you've got to, come on. I mean, you've got to think, right? VC people are looking for a 10 times return, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The typical client volume band for a hardware-manufacturing consultancy is between 5,000 and a million units, which is where the process knowledge is concentrated; companies building a hundred units sit outside that band.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of our customers I'd say are typically looking to build between 5,000 and a million units. And for us, that's the area we know that the best as well.
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Founders commonly make irreversible legal-structure errors at the outset: one hardware founder identified incorporating as a corporation with a board and shareholders, rather than forming an LLC, as her single largest early mistake.
claims.quote_verbatim: one huge mistake that I made in the beginning that I talk openly about to anybody who's thinking about going into, um, running a hardware startup or any startup for that matter is I thought I needed to incorporate instead of becoming an LLC.
claims.speaker: Christina Cyr

claims.claim_text: Startups demand both breadth and depth from the same engineer, which is what makes them hard; when a startup succeeds and becomes a large company, the same engineer is often narrowed back to a small piece of the system they originally designed.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's less pigeonholing in startups. You have to do breadth, but you also have to do depth, which is what makes them so hard.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The distinguishing behaviour of people who succeed at running businesses is persistence at a chosen activity rather than initial brilliance; most start something, such as a blog, and let it taper off.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're going to do something, just keep doing it. And a lot of people, they'll start a blog and it tapers out. But the successful people are the ones who are able to focus and keep on doing what has to be done.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: Venture returns come from a handful of large winners against thousands of investments that failed completely, so the visible successes are unrepresentative of the outcome distribution a founder is entering.
claims.quote_verbatim: they got a dozen huge winners, but there's literally thousands they invested in that flopped and lost a hundred percent of their money
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Depending on the survey, between sixty and eighty percent of traditional software startups fail; hardware startups carry additional risk on top of that baseline.
claims.quote_verbatim: a traditional software startup, you know, 60, 70, up to 80% of them, depending on which survey you read, die of natural causes, right?
claims.speaker: Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: A hardware startup's first fifteen employees frequently span eight to ten distinct engineering disciplines that must be coordinated effectively, and the capital requirement is correspondingly higher; faced with a software and a hardware investment at the same projected return, most venture investors take the software one because the risk is lower.
claims.quote_verbatim: just think of the capital requirements and the fact that in the first 15 employees, you often can represent eight, nine, 10 distinct disciplines that must come together effectively to do a very, you know, difficult thing, which is to bring together hardware and software. They, by their inherent nature, are doing software and then adding hardware on top of it. And so there is more risk associated with a hardware startup.
claims.speaker: Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: The failure-to-success ratio in consumer hardware has been skewed far enough toward failure to deter venture investors from the consumer category in favour of industrial and business-facing hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ratio of death to success is, is so far skewed to failure right now that it really scares venture capitalists away from consumer
claims.speaker: Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: In a small hardware startup one engineer typically absorbs supply-chain, test-engineering and fixture work alongside design, including pressing leadership to commit to fourteen-week lead-time parts long before the build — a warning that does not land because startups run reactively.
claims.quote_verbatim: I found myself going to the leadership and being like, guys, we have a long lead time parks, 14 weeks, got to order it now. And I was just like, come on, come on. I'm like doing the job of like a supply chain person, the test person, like creating all these test fixtures, everything from scratch. And I'm like the only person doing this is like, what is this?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Hardware startups plan poorly for the long term because the software startup model they inherit is cash-light while hardware is cash-heavy: without the cash flow to commit early to parts, planning beyond the immediate customer problem is difficult.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's the downside to hardware startups in general is that they're not built for, you know, the software model is so like cash light and hardware is so cash heavy
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: An engineer joining a startup should hold three to five months of living expenses in savings, because the downside outcomes — sudden layoff, or pay cut to minimum wage pending a funding round — arrive without warning and are not visible in the recruiting pitch.
claims.quote_verbatim: have at least three to five months of expenses and savings. We're when working at a startup because people will paint it in the most beautiful picture. And then you start working there. And it's just like surprise you're laid off or surprise we're paying you minimum wage because we haven't got a round of funding yet.
claims.speaker: Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: A company's stated runway overstates the job security it provides: management will not spend down to zero, so a two-year runway typically produces a headcount cut at the one-year mark and another at six months in order to stretch the remaining cash.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if you have a company that has like a two year runway, they don't want to use it. You know, it's not like they're like, well, go down to zero. It's like, no, no, no. We get to one year. There's a big chop coming. You know, if we get to six months, there's another big chop coming because we got to stretch it out. And it's like that's what I didn't quite get. I didn't quite grasp. It was just like cash by itself is not a good indicator of how fast it will be spending it.
claims.speaker: Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: An accelerator is not a source of hardware engineering expertise; founders who join expecting to be taught hardware have misread the offering, which is funding, focus, peer group and help scaling.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't go to Y Combinator for them to teach you about hardware. Right. Like if you're going to Y Combinator for them to teach you about hardware, you're doing it wrong. Like, I mean, that's not, that should not be the expectation at all.
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: From a customer's perspective, a venture-funded tool vendor has no good outcome: an IPO redirects the company toward growth and revenue extraction, and an acquisition usually ends in shutdown or absorption into another product.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're dealing with a VC funded company, there is no outcome that is good for you as a customer. That's right. None of them. If the company IPOs, which will likely not happen. That's right. Then they will go on to surge growth and revenues. This is not good for you. If they get acquired, they will probably get shut down or merged into something.

claims.claim_text: Around seven and a half million dollars of venture funding allowed one hardware company the latitude to develop a product properly instead of rushing it to market on crowdfunding timelines — a case where capital bought schedule rather than scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: they got, I think, seven and a half million dollars venture capital funding or something of that order. I don't know if it was more than... That was one of them. I don't know if they got extra on top of that, but that gave them the luxury to actually spend time to do it properly rather than rush it to Kickstarter market
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wow, Dave REALLY likes Top Gun

claims.claim_text: Startups compress learning because speed is the deciding factor and mistakes are visible: an engineer can make an error that costs the company a million dollars in full view of everyone, which is unusual exposure compared with a large organisation.
claims.quote_verbatim: It is a good chance to, like, fail on stage a little bit in a way where, like, you're going to mess something up, you know, in a way that, like, everybody in the company sees it and it costs, like, a million dollars. And you, like, that's you. You did that. Todd Bailey. Todd Bailey did that. He cost the company a million dollars.
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey

claims.claim_text: Arduino took around fifty million dollars of venture capital, which sets a floor on any acceptable acquisition price far above the company's earnings; selling roughly two million boards a year with about eighty percent of income from hardware sales, the margin does not support a valuation in the hundreds of millions.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was $50 million venture capital that went into Arduino, right? That means they're not going to sell out for anything under like 200 mil, right? So I reckon the deal is in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars. And if you look at, and I ran the numbers, Arduino, I checked, Arduino sell about 2 million boards a year. Most of their income comes from hardware. About 80% of their income comes from hardware sales still.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Before restarting a consumer hardware company, one founder listed everything he liked and disliked about running a hardware startup and found the dislike list substantially longer — an exercise that shaped which parts of the model, including venture funding, he chose to avoid the second time.
claims.quote_verbatim: I wrote a list down of all the things that I love about doing hardware and all the things that I do not love. About doing hardware and specifically a hardware startup, like one that's, you know, making consumer electronics and selling it to people. The list of things that I didn't like was much longer than the things that I did like.
claims.speaker: Eric Migicovsky
claims.episode_title: Shiny New Pebble with Eric Migicovsky
